chunks: By the chain from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad from Hariz from Zurara who said:

I said to him: If a man falls asleep while in a state of wudu, does the 'khafqah' (a light sleep/dozing) and the 'khafqatan' (two light sleeps) oblige him to renew wudu? He said: O Zurara, the eye may sleep while the heart and the ear are awake. When the eye, the ear, and the heart all sleep, then wudu becomes obligatory. I said: What if something moves him to his side and he is not aware of it? He said: No [wudu is not broken], unless he is certain that he has fallen asleep, until a clear matter comes from that [indicating sleep]. Otherwise, he remains upon certainty of his wudu, and certainty is never broken by doubt, but it is broken by another certainty.

key_terms.الْقَلْب: Al-Qalb (the heart, referring to the faculty of consciousness/sleep)

ai.seo_question: Does light sleep or dozing invalidate wudu in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from the Tadhhib clarifies the jurisprudential criteria for wudu invalidation by distinguishing between light dozing and deep sleep, emphasizing that the 'heart' (consciousness) must be dormant alongside the senses. It further establishes the foundational legal maxim that certainty (yaqin) is not broken by mere doubt (shakk) but only by a new certainty, a principle widely applied in Shia fiqh for ritual purity. The narration highlights the practical application of this rule when one is uncertain if they moved or slept during the night.

en.ammaar-muslim: 3. [3/96] al-Tahdhib: By the chain to al-Husayn b. Sa`id from Hammad from Hariz from Zurara who said:

I said to him: a man in Wudhu falls asleep – closing his eyes for a beat or two – does this mean that he is obliged to renew Wudhu? he said: O Zurara, the eye may sleep while the heart and the ear are awake, only when the eye, the ear and the heart all sleep does Wudhu become obligatory, I said: what if something moves near him while he is not even aware of it, he said: no [that does not mean he has to renew Wudhu], unless he is certain that he has fallen asleep and unless there manifests a clear sign indicating that, if not then he was certain about his initial Wudhu and certainty is never overriden by doubt rather what overrides it [certainty] is another certainty [he become sure of a new event].
